{{Short description|Algorithm used in modular arithmetic}}
The '''Tonelli–Shanks''' [[algorithm]] (referred to by Shanks as the RESSOL algorithm) is used in [[modular arithmetic]] to solve for ''r'' in a congruence of the form ''r''<sup>2</sup> ≡ ''n'' (mod ''p''), where ''p'' is a [[prime number|prime]]: that is, to find a square root of ''n'' modulo ''p''.

The Tonelli–Shanks algorithm cannot be used for composite moduli: finding square roots modulo composite numbers is a [[computational problem]] equivalent to [[integer factorization]].<ref>Oded Goldreich, ''Computational complexity: a conceptual perspective'', Cambridge University Press, 2008, p. 588.</ref>

An equivalent, but slightly more redundant version of this algorithm was developed by
[[:it:Alberto Tonelli|Alberto Tonelli]]<ref name="DiekertKufleitner2016">{{cite book
|title=Discrete Algebraic Methods: Arithmetic, Cryptography, Automata and Groups
|author1=Volker Diekert|author2=Manfred Kufleitner|author3=Gerhard Rosenberger|author4=Ulrich Hertrampf
|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OB9BDAAAQBAJ&pg=PT163
|date=24 May 2016|publisher=De Gruyter|isbn=978-3-11-041632-9|pages=163–165}}
</ref><ref name="dickson">{{cite book
|author=Leonard Eugene Dickson
|title=History of the Theory of Numbers
|year=1919
|volume=1
|pages=[https://archive.org/details/historyoftheoryo01dick/page/215 215]–216
|publisher=Washington, Carnegie Institution of Washington
|url=https://archive.org/details/historyoftheoryo01dick
}}
</ref>
in 1891. The version discussed here was developed independently by [[Daniel Shanks]] in 1973, who explained:

<blockquote>My tardiness in learning of these historical references was because I had lent Volume 1 of [[Leonard Eugene Dickson|Dickson's]] [[History of the Theory of Numbers|History]] to a friend and it was never returned.<ref>Daniel Shanks. Five Number-theoretic Algorithms. Proceedings of the Second Manitoba Conference on Numerical Mathematics. Pp. 51–70. 1973.</ref>
</blockquote>

According to Dickson,<ref name="dickson"/> Tonelli's algorithm can take square roots of ''x'' modulo prime powers ''p<sup>λ</sup>'' apart from primes.

==Core ideas==

Given a non-zero <math>n</math> and a prime <math>p > 2</math> (which will always be odd), [[Euler's criterion]] tells us that <math>n</math> has a square root (i.e., <math>n</math> is a [[quadratic residue]]) [[if and only if]]:

:<math>n^{\frac{p-1}{2}} \equiv 1 \pmod p</math>.

In contrast, if a number <math>z</math> has no square root (is a non-residue), Euler's criterion tells us that:

:<math>z^{\frac{p-1}{2}} \equiv -1 \pmod p</math>.

It is not hard to find such <math>z</math>, because half of the integers between 1 and <math>p-1</math> have this property.  So we assume that we have access to such a non-residue.

By (normally) dividing by 2 repeatedly, we can write <math>p-1</math> as <math>Q 2^S</math>, where <math>Q</math> is odd.  Note that if we try

:<math>R \equiv n^{\frac{Q+1}{2}} \pmod p</math>,

then <math>R^2 \equiv n^{Q+1} = (n)(n^Q) \pmod p</math>.  If <math>t \equiv n^Q \equiv 1 \pmod p</math>, then <math>R</math> is a square root of <math>n</math>.  Otherwise, for <math>M = S</math>, we have <math>R</math> and <math>t</math> satisfying:

* <math>R^2 \equiv nt \pmod p</math>; and
* <math>t</math> is a <math>2^{M-1}</math>-th root of 1 (because <math>t^{2^{M-1}} = t^{2^{S-1}} \equiv n^{Q 2^{S-1}} = n^{\frac{p-1}{2}}</math>).

If, given a choice of <math>R</math> and <math>t</math> for a particular <math>M</math> satisfying the above (where <math>R</math> is not a square root of <math>n</math>), we can easily calculate another <math>R</math> and <math>t</math> for <math>M - 1</math> such that the above relations hold, then we can repeat this until <math>t</math> becomes a <math>2^0</math>-th root of 1, i.e., <math>t = 1</math>.  At that point <math>R</math> is a square root of <math>n</math>.

We can check whether <math>t</math> is a <math>2^{M-2}</math>-th root of 1 by squaring it <math>M-2</math> times and check whether it is 1.  If it is, then we do not need to do anything, as the same choice of <math>R</math> and <math>t</math> works.  But if it is not, <math>t^{2^{M-2}}</math> must be -1 (because squaring it gives 1, and there can only be two square roots 1 and -1 of 1 modulo <math>p</math>).

To find a new pair of <math>R</math> and <math>t</math>, we can multiply <math>R</math> by a factor <math>b</math>, to be determined.  Then <math>t</math> must be multiplied by a factor <math>b^2</math> to keep <math>R^2 \equiv nt \pmod p</math>.  So, when <math>t^{2^{M-2}}</math> is -1, we need to find a factor <math>b^2</math> so that <math>tb^2</math> is a <math>2^{M-2}</math>-th root of 1, or equivalently <math>b^2</math> is a <math>2^{M-2}</math>-th root of -1.

The trick here is to make use of <math>z</math>, the known non-residue.  The Euler's criterion applied to <math>z</math> shown above says that <math>z^Q</math> is a <math>2^{S-1}</math>-th root of -1.  So by squaring <math>z^Q</math> repeatedly, we have access to a sequence of <math>2^i</math>-th roots of -1.  We can select the right one to serve as <math>b</math>.  With a little bit of variable maintenance and trivial case compression, the algorithm below emerges naturally.

== The algorithm ==
Operations and comparisons on elements of the [[multiplicative group of integers modulo n|multiplicative group of integers modulo p]] <math>\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}</math> are implicitly mod ''p''.

'''Inputs''':
* ''p'', a prime
* ''n'', an element of <math>\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}</math> such that solutions to the congruence ''r''<sup>2</sup> = ''n'' exist; when this is so we say that ''n'' is a [[quadratic residue]] mod ''p''.

'''Outputs''':
* ''r'' in <math>\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}</math> such that ''r''<sup>2</sup> = ''n''
'''Algorithm''':
# By factoring out powers of 2, find ''Q'' and ''S'' such that <math>p-1=Q 2^S</math> with ''Q'' odd
# Search for a ''z''  in <math>\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}</math> which is a quadratic non-residue
#* Half of the elements in the set will be quadratic non-residues
#* Candidates can be tested with [[Euler's criterion]] or by finding the [[Jacobi symbol]]
# Let
#:<math>\begin{align}
  M &\leftarrow S   \\
  c &\leftarrow z^Q \\
  t &\leftarrow n^Q \\
  R &\leftarrow n^\frac{Q+1}{2}
\end{align}</math>
# Loop:
#* If ''t'' = 0, return ''r'' = ''0''
#* If ''t'' = 1, return ''r'' = ''R''
#* Otherwise, use repeated squaring to find the least ''i'', 0 &lt; ''i'' &lt; ''M'', such that <math>t^{2^i} = 1</math>
#* Let <math>b \leftarrow c^{2^{M-i-1}}</math>, and set
#*:<math>\begin{align}
  M &\leftarrow i    \\
  c &\leftarrow b^2  \\
  t &\leftarrow tb^2 \\
  R &\leftarrow Rb
\end{align}</math>

Once you have solved the congruence with ''r'' the second solution is <math> -r \pmod p</math>. If the least ''i'' such that <math>t^{2^i} = 1</math> is ''M'', then no solution to the congruence exists, i.e. ''n'' is not a quadratic residue.

This is most useful when ''p'' ≡ 1 (mod 4).

For primes such that ''p'' ≡ 3 (mod 4), this problem has possible solutions <math>r = \pm n^{\frac{p+1}{4}}\pmod p</math>. If these satisfy <math>r^2 \equiv n \pmod p</math>, they are the only solutions. If not, <math>r^2 \equiv -n \pmod p</math>, ''n'' is a quadratic non-residue, and there are no solutions.

==Proof==

We can show that at the start of each iteration of the loop the following  [[loop invariant]]s hold:

* <math>c^{2^{M-1}} = -1</math>
* <math>t^{2^{M-1}} = 1</math>
* <math>R^2 = tn</math>

Initially:

* <math>c^{2^{M-1}} = z^{Q2^{S-1}} = z^\frac{p-1}{2} = -1</math> (since ''z'' is a quadratic nonresidue, per Euler's criterion)
* <math>t^{2^{M-1}} = n^{Q2^{S-1}} = n^\frac{p-1}{2} = 1</math> (since ''n'' is a quadratic residue)
* <math>R^2 = n^{Q+1} = tn</math>

At each iteration, with ''M' '', ''c' '', ''t' '', ''R' '' the new values replacing ''M'', ''c'', ''t'', ''R'':

* <math>c'^{2^{M'-1}} = (b^2)^{2^{i-1}} = c^{2^{M-i}2^{i-1}} = c^{2^{M-1}} = -1</math>
* <math>t'^{2^{M'-1}} = (tb^2)^{2^{i-1}} = t^{2^{i-1}}b^{2^i} = -1 \cdot -1 = 1</math>
** <math>t^{2^{i-1}} = -1</math> since we have that <math>t^{2^i} = 1</math> but <math>t^{2^{i-1}} \neq 1</math> (''i'' is the least value such that <math>t^{2^i} = 1</math>)
** <math>b^{2^i} = c^{2^{M-i-1}2^i}= c^{2^{M-1}} = -1</math>
* <math>R'^2 = R^2b^2 = tnb^2 = t'n</math>

From <math>t^{2^{M-1}} = 1</math> and the test against ''t'' = 1 at the start of the loop, we see that we will always find an ''i'' in 0 &lt; ''i'' &lt; ''M'' such that <math>t^{2^i} = 1</math>. ''M'' is strictly smaller on each iteration, and thus the algorithm is guaranteed to halt. When we hit the condition ''t'' = 1 and halt, the last loop invariant implies that ''R''<sup>2</sup> = ''n''.

===Order of ''t''===

We can alternately express the loop invariants using the [[order (group theory)|order]] of the elements:

* <math>\operatorname{ord}(c) = 2^M</math>
* <math>\operatorname{ord}(t) | 2^{M-1}</math>
* <math>R^2 = tn</math> as before

Each step of the algorithm moves ''t'' into a smaller subgroup by measuring the exact order of ''t'' and multiplying it by an element of the same order.

==Example==
Solving the congruence ''r''<sup>2</sup> ≡ 5 (mod 41). 41 is prime as required and 41 ≡ 1 (mod 4). 5 is a quadratic residue by Euler's criterion: <math>5^{\frac{41-1}{2}} = 5^{20} = 1</math> (as before, operations in <math>(\mathbb{Z}/41\mathbb{Z})^\times</math> are implicitly mod 41).

# <math>p-1 = 40 =  5 \cdot 2^3 </math> so <math>Q \leftarrow 5</math>, <math>S \leftarrow 3</math>
# Find a value for z:
#* <math>2^{\frac{41-1}{2}} = 1</math>, so 2 is a quadratic residue by Euler's criterion.
#* <math>3^{\frac{41-1}{2}} = 40 = -1</math>, so 3 is a quadratic nonresidue: set <math>z \leftarrow 3</math>
# Set
#*<math>M \leftarrow S = 3</math>
#*<math>c \leftarrow z^Q = 3^5 = 38</math>
#*<math>t \leftarrow n^Q = 5^5 = 9</math>
#*<math>R \leftarrow n^{\frac{Q+1}{2}} = 5^{\frac{5+1}{2}} = 2</math>
# Loop:
#* First iteration:
#** <math>t \neq 1</math>, so we're not finished
#** <math>t^{2^1} = 40</math>, <math>t^{2^2} = 1</math> so <math>i \leftarrow 2</math>
#** <math>b \leftarrow c^{2^{M-i-1}} = 38^{2^{3-2-1}} = 38</math>
#** <math>M \leftarrow i = 2</math>
#** <math>c \leftarrow b^2 = 38^2 = 9</math>
#** <math>t \leftarrow tb^2 = 9 \cdot 9 = 40</math>
#** <math>R \leftarrow Rb = 2 \cdot 38 = 35</math>
#* Second iteration:
#** <math>t \neq 1</math>, so we're still not finished
#** <math>t^{2^1} = 1</math> so <math>i \leftarrow 1</math>
#** <math>b \leftarrow c^{2^{M-i-1}} = 9^{2^{2-1-1}} = 9</math>
#** <math>M \leftarrow i = 1</math>
#** <math>c \leftarrow b^2 = 9^2 = 40</math>
#** <math>t \leftarrow tb^2 = 40 \cdot 40 = 1</math>
#** <math>R \leftarrow Rb = 35 \cdot 9 = 28</math>
#* Third iteration:
#** <math>t = 1</math>, and we are finished; return <math>r = R = 28</math>

Indeed, 28<sup>2</sup> ≡ 5 (mod 41) and (−28)<sup>2</sup> ≡ 13<sup>2</sup> ≡ 5 (mod 41). So the algorithm yields the two solutions to our congruence.

==Speed of the algorithm==
The Tonelli–Shanks algorithm requires (on average over all possible input (quadratic residues and quadratic nonresidues))

:<math>2m+2k+\frac{S(S-1)}{4} +\frac{1}{2^{S-1}} - 9</math>

modular multiplications, where <math>m</math> is the number of digits in the binary representation of <math>p</math> and <math>k</math> is the number of ones in the binary representation of <math>p</math>. If the required quadratic nonresidue <math>z</math> is to be found by checking if a randomly taken number <math>y</math> is a quadratic nonresidue, it requires (on average) <math>2</math> computations of the [[Legendre symbol]].<ref>{{cite book | doi=10.1007/3-540-45995-2_38 | chapter=Square Roots Modulo P | title=LATIN 2002: Theoretical Informatics | series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science | date=2002 | last1=Tornaría | first1=Gonzalo | volume=2286 | pages=430–434 | isbn=978-3-540-43400-9 }}</ref> The average of two computations of the [[Legendre symbol]] are explained as follows: <math>y</math> is a quadratic residue with chance <math>\tfrac{\tfrac{p+1}{2}}{p} = \tfrac{1 + \tfrac{1}{p}}{2}</math>, which is smaller than <math>1</math> but <math>\geq \tfrac{1}{2}</math>, so we will on average need to check if a <math>y</math> is a quadratic residue two times.

This shows essentially that the Tonelli–Shanks algorithm works very well if the modulus <math>p</math> is random, that is, if <math>S</math> is not particularly large with respect to the number of digits in the binary representation of <math>p</math>. As written above, [[Cipolla's algorithm]] works better than Tonelli–Shanks if (and only if) <math>S(S-1) > 8m + 20</math>.
However, if one instead uses Sutherland's algorithm to perform the discrete logarithm computation in the 2-Sylow subgroup of <math>\mathbb{F}_p^{\ast}</math>, one may replace <math>S(S-1)</math> with an expression that is asymptotically bounded by <math>O(S\log S/\log\log S)</math>.<ref>{{citation |last=Sutherland |first=Andrew V. |year=2011 |title=Structure computation and discrete logarithms in finite abelian p-groups |journal=Mathematics of Computation |volume=80 |issue=273 |pages=477–500 |doi=10.1090/s0025-5718-10-02356-2|arxiv=0809.3413 |s2cid=13940949 }}</ref>  Explicitly, one computes <math>e</math> such that <math>c^e\equiv n^Q</math> and then <math>R\equiv c^{-e/2} n^{(Q+1)/2}</math> satisfies <math>R^2\equiv n</math> (note that <math>e</math> is a multiple of 2 because <math>n</math> is a quadratic residue).

The algorithm requires us to find a quadratic nonresidue <math>z</math>. There is no known deterministic algorithm that runs in polynomial time for finding such a <math>z</math>. However, if the [[generalized Riemann hypothesis]] is true, there exists a quadratic nonresidue <math>z < 2\ln^2{p}</math>,<ref>{{Citation |last=Bach |first=Eric |year=1990 |title=Explicit bounds for primality testing and related problems |journal=Mathematics of Computation |volume=55 |issue=191 |pages=355–380 |jstor=2008811 |doi=10.2307/2008811|doi-access=free }}</ref> making it possible to check every <math>z</math> up to that limit and find a suitable <math>z</math> within [[polynomial time]]. Keep in mind, however, that this is a worst-case scenario; in general, <math>z</math> is found in on average 2 trials as stated above.

== Uses ==
The Tonelli–Shanks algorithm can (naturally) be used for any process in which square roots modulo a prime are necessary. For example, it can be used for finding points on [[elliptic curves]]. It is also useful for the computations in the [[Rabin signature algorithm]] and in the sieving step of the [[quadratic sieve]].

== Generalizations ==
Tonelli–Shanks can be generalized to any [[cyclic group]] (instead of <math>(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times</math>) and to ''k''th roots for arbitrary integer ''k'', in particular to taking the ''k''th root of an element of a [[finite field]].<ref>Adleman, L. M., K. Manders, and G. Miller: 1977, `On taking roots in finite fields'. In: 18th IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science. pp. 175-177</ref>

If many square-roots must be done in the same cyclic group and S is not too large, a table of square-roots of the elements of 2-power order can be prepared in advance and the algorithm simplified and sped up as follows.
# Factor out powers of 2 from ''p'' − 1, defining ''Q'' and ''S'' as: <math>p-1 = Q2^S</math> with ''Q'' odd.
# Let <math>R \leftarrow n^{\frac{Q+1}{2}}, t\leftarrow n^Q \equiv R^2/n</math>
# Find <math>b</math> from the table such that <math>b^2 \equiv t </math> and set <math>R \equiv R/b</math>
#return ''R''.

=== Tonelli's algorithm will work on mod ''p<sup>λ</sup>'' ===

According to Dickson's "Theory of Numbers"<ref name="dickson"/>

<blockquote>
A. Tonelli<ref>"Accademia nazionale dei Lincei, Rome. Rendiconti, (5), 1, 1892, 116-120."</ref> gave an explicit formula for the roots of <math>x^{2}=c \pmod{ p^{\lambda}}</math><ref name="dickson"/>
</blockquote>

The Dickson reference shows the following formula for the square root of <math>x^{2}\bmod{p^{\lambda}}</math>.

:when <math>p=4\cdot7+1</math>, or <math>s=2</math> (s must be 2 for this equation) and <math>a=7</math> such that <math>29=2^{2}\cdot7+1</math>
::for <math>x^{2}\bmod{p^{\lambda}}\equiv c</math> then
:::<math>x \bmod{p^{\lambda}}\equiv \pm (c^{a}+3)^{\beta}\cdot c^{(\beta+1)/2}</math> where <math>\beta \equiv a\cdot p^{\lambda-1}</math>

Noting that <math>23^{2} \bmod{ 29^{3}}\equiv 529</math> and noting that <math>\beta = 7\cdot29^{2}</math> then

:<math>(529^{7} + 3)^{7\cdot 29^{2}}\cdot 529^{(7\cdot29^{2} + 1)/2}\bmod{ 29^{3}}\equiv 24366 \equiv -23</math>

To take another example: <math>2333^{2} \bmod{ 29^{3}}\equiv 4142</math> and

::<math>(4142^{7} + 3)^{7 \cdot29^{2}}\cdot 4142^{(7\cdot29^{2} + 1)/2}\bmod{ 29^{3}}\equiv 2333</math>

Dickson also attributes the following equation to Tonelli:

:<math>X\bmod{p^{\lambda}}\equiv x^{p^{\lambda-1}}\cdot c^{(p^{\lambda}-2p^{\lambda-1}+1)/2}</math> where <math>X^{2}\bmod{p^{\lambda}}\equiv c</math> and <math>x^{2}\bmod{p}\equiv c</math>;

Using <math>p=23</math> and using the modulus of <math>p^{3}</math> the math follows:

:<math>1115^{2}\bmod{ 23^{3}}=2191</math>

First, find the modular square root mod <math>p</math> which can be done by the regular Tonelli algorithm for one or the other roots:

:<math>1115^{2}\bmod{ 23}\equiv 6</math> and thus <math>\sqrt{6}\bmod{23}\equiv 11</math>

And applying Tonelli's equation (see above):

:<math>11^{23^{2}}\cdot 2191^{(23^{3} - 2 \cdot23^{2} + 1)/2}\bmod {23^{3}} \equiv 1115</math>

Dickson's reference<ref name="dickson"/> clearly shows that Tonelli's algorithm works on moduli of <math>p^{\lambda}</math>.
